name: Erik Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two CNC machining centres at Kestrel Precision. CNC means the machine cuts metal from a program, so I load the aluminium blocks, set the tools, run the program and measure what comes out. We make brackets and housings, some for aircraft, some for hospital equipment. Day shift, seven till half three. Most of the day is measuring, honestly, because a part that's two hundredths of a millimetre out goes in the scrap bin.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle. When a part keeps coming out wrong and you work out it's the tool heating up after the tenth one, that's a good day. I use an AI chat tool every day now, on my phone at break, to check a program change or explain a bit of a manual that's in German. What wears me out is the paperwork for the aircraft jobs, and my wife Mira's on nights at the hospital, so I do the school run on my own most weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a useful helper and nothing more. Probably post something about how the people selling it got rich and the rest of us got a slightly better search engine. I'm a bit of a shouter online, Mira says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd be good news, if I'm honest. I like the tools, I'd keep using them, and my job stays. I'd be a bit disappointed, I'll admit it. I was curious where it'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep using the chat tool for programs, maybe get Kestrel to pay for a proper version instead of the free one on my phone. We'd keep the savings where they are, about three months, and fix up Lukas's bike for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like a film that had a good trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want Kestrel to pay for a proper version. Would they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not unless it saved them money they could see. I'd write it up, how many scrapped parts I'd avoided. Our manager likes numbers on one sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about your work that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork, and that we've got no union at Kestrel. I've been talking about it with a few of the lads for a year. That'd still need doing, AI or no AI.

S0.say: It's a useful helper and nothing more. The people selling it got rich and the rest of us got a slightly better search engine, which is about what I'd post.
S0.think: For me it'd be good news: I like the tools, I'd keep using them, and my job stays. I'll admit I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was curious where it would go.
S0.do: Keeps working and keeps using the chat tool for program checks, writing up scrap savings to ask Kestrel to pay for a proper version. Leaves the three months of savings alone and fixes up Lukas's bike.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a film that had a good trailer.
S0.quote: Calm. A bit flat, like a film that had a good trailer.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is the rare operator who'd be slightly let down if AI fizzled. He already uses it daily and thinks in terms of evidence his manager would accept. His bigger ongoing project is getting a union into a non-union shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a say in how it comes in, and that's why we need a union at Kestrel. I'd say it at work and online. I'm not against the robots, I'm against the owners keeping every penny they save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do all right. The machines will need people who understand both the cutting and the software, and that's me more than most. The ones I'd worry for are the lads who load and unload and don't touch the programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Kestrel to put me on the robot loading cell they've been quoting for. I'd do a robotics short course at the technical college, evenings, it's about eight hundred, and pay it myself if they won't. And I'd push the union thing harder, get the sign-up cards out in the first six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. A bit excited. Then guilty about being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I'm on the robot cell, it's because the cell replaced two of my mates. Jonny loads my machines on nights. He's got three kids. I can't pretend I'd be the hero of that story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay eight hundred yourself. What would that come out of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings, a bit. Or I'd skip the new phone. Mira would say do it, she's watched hospital software change her job twice already and she says the ones who learned it early got the better shifts.

S1.say: Workers need a say in how this comes in, which is why we need a union at Kestrel. I'm not against the robots, I'm against the owners keeping every penny they save.
S1.think: I think I'd do all right, because the machines will need people who understand both the cutting and the software. The ones I'd worry for are the lads who only load and unload.
S1.do: Asks to run Kestrel's planned robot loading cell and pays around 800 for an evening robotics course at the technical college if the company won't. Gets union sign-up cards out within six months.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, then guilty about the excitement.
S1.quote: I can't pretend I'd be the hero of that story.
S1.fieldNote: Erik is calm here because his skills fit the change, but he's honest that his gain comes from colleagues' loss. That guilt pushes him harder towards organising a union. His wife's experience with hospital software shapes his view that early learners get the better deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs pausing or at least a law that shares the gains, now. I'd be loud about it online and I'd be at any march going. Two years is not a transition, it's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years worries me even with my skills. If AI can program the machines and robots can load them, what am I? The bloke who knows the job better than the robot for about eighteen months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to set up the robots at Kestrel, because if it's coming I'd rather be the one who knows how it works, and that buys time. I'd put everything spare into savings, try to get to six months. I'd push for the union to win a deal on payouts before the cuts start, and I'd back whoever's promising a share of the gains for workers, like a robot tax that pays people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. My head's working fast but my stomach isn't keeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what does knowing the tools actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year longer than the others. That's not nothing with a mortgage, a year is twelve payments. But I'm not kidding myself it's a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lukas? He's fourteen.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the truth, he'd see through anything else. He wants to be a mechanic. I'd say keep learning, keep curious, but don't bet everything on one trade. That's hard advice to give when you don't know the answer.

S2.say: This needs pausing, or at least a law that shares the gains, now. Two years is not a transition, it's a cliff, and I'd say so online and at any march going.
S2.think: Two years worries me even with my skills. If AI can program the machines and robots can load them, I'm the bloke who knows the job better than the robot for about eighteen months.
S2.do: Volunteers to set up Kestrel's robots to stay useful longer and pushes all spare money into savings towards six months. Presses for a union payout deal before cuts and backs a robot tax that pays workers.
S2.feel: Tense, with his head working fast and his stomach not keeping up.
S2.quote: If AI can program the machines and robots can load them, what am I? The bloke who knows the job better than the robot for about eighteen months.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's adaptability buys him time, not safety, and he's clear about that. He'd help bring in the robots and campaign against the way they're brought in at the same time. The advice to Lukas, keep curious but don't bet on one trade, was hard for him to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance to do this right: shorter weeks, retraining, a share of the profits. I'd be pushing for it everywhere, and I'd say people should get organised now while they still have jobs to strike from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a lot better for me. I could get properly qualified on robotics and be the one maintaining the robots across a few factories, not just ours. That job lasts longer than mine, maybe not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the two-year technician diploma at the college, part-time, starting next September. I'd save hard, six months if I can. I'd get the union recognised at Kestrel in year one, because once the robots arrive nobody listens to you. And I'd vote on it, campaign a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like busy-uneasy. I'd have a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be maintaining robots across factories. Doesn't AGI eventually do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. I'm not daft. But that's year eight or nine, not year two. You've got to get from here to there, and Lukas will be through school by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Mira's nights fit with a diploma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. Two evenings a week at college and her on nights means my mum has the kids twice a week. She'd do it, she'd moan, but she'd do it.

S3.say: Five years is a real chance to do this right, with shorter weeks, retraining and a share of the profits. People should get organised now while they still have jobs to strike from.
S3.think: Five years is a lot better for me, because I could get properly qualified and maintain robots across several factories. That job lasts longer than mine, maybe not forever.
S3.do: Starts a part-time two-year technician diploma next September, with his mum minding the kids twice a week. Saves towards six months, gets the union recognised at Kestrel in year one, and votes and campaigns on the issue.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, with a list of things to do.
S3.quote: People should get organised now while they still have jobs to strike from.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Erik sees a clear bridge job in robot maintenance, while admitting AGI eventually takes that too. His plan depends on family help, his mum taking the kids twice a week. He links timing to his son finishing school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no excuses. We could have a four-day week, money from the robots going to everyone, proper planning. I'd say it and I'd keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is long enough that I could change fields twice if I had to. I'd be fifty-three at the end. I worry more about what the whole thing does to people who aren't like me, who don't like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the diploma, then move into robot installation, maybe with one of the firms that sells the cells, in year three or four. I'd stay in the union and help organise people in the new job too. And I'd put time into campaigns for a basic income, because by year ten the question isn't my job, it's everyone's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end. Fine about the road there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry more for others than yourself. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother-in-law Piotr. He works in a warehouse and hates computers. He'd be the one sitting at home in year ten, and he'd blame himself. I'd be the one in the family trying to drag him to a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the four-day week and shared money didn't happen, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be one of the lucky ones for a while and angry the whole time. I've got no plan for a world that just tells most people to go away.

S4.say: Ten years means no excuses: a four-day week, money from the robots going to everyone, proper planning. I'd say it and keep saying it.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough that I could change fields twice if I had to. I worry more about what it does to people who aren't like me, who don't like change.
S4.do: Finishes the diploma and moves into robot installation with a firm that sells robot cells around year three or four. Organises in the new job and campaigns for a basic income.
S4.feel: Uneasy about where it ends, fine about the road there.
S4.quote: I've got no plan for a world that just tells most people to go away.
S4.fieldNote: Erik's personal worry fades with time, but his political worry grows. He sees himself as the family member who'd drag his brother-in-law to a course. The gap between his own safety and his fear for others is the clearest thing about him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm adaptable, but you can't adapt to a cliff. What would help is a law, before it happens, that says the money saved by automation goes partly to the people it replaces, and union recognition in every factory, so we're not negotiating one by one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people what they'd miss. I'd miss the puzzle. The day the tool's heating up after the tenth part and nobody knows why, and then I do. A robot solving that won't feel what I feel when I solve it.

headlineQuote: A robot solving that won't feel what I feel when I solve it.
portrait: Erik Novak, 43, runs two CNC machining centres at Kestrel Precision, making aluminium parts for aircraft and hospital equipment. He uses AI every day, likes the puzzle of the work, and is trying to get a union into his non-union shop. He stays calm through the milder pictures and even feels a guilty excitement about running robots, but AGI in two years makes him anxious because his skills only buy him months. With five or ten years he plans a technician diploma and a move into robot installation, while his worry shifts from himself to people like his brother-in-law who hate change.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because even an adaptable person can't adapt to a cliff.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring part of the money saved by automation to go to the people it replaces, plus union recognition in every factory so workers aren't negotiating one by one.
